steps.prompt: Pick a two-digit number, reverse its digits, and subtract the smaller from the larger. Try a few. What do all your answers have in common?

cards.title: Write the digits as letters
cards.body: A two-digit number with tens digit $a$ and units digit $b$ is $10a + b$ (not $ab$, which means $a \times b$). Its reversal is $10b + a$. A three-digit number is $100a + 10b + c$. Remember: $a$ can't be $0$, and every digit is a whole number from $0$ to $9$.

cards.title: Worked example: reversing
cards.problem: A two-digit number minus its reversal is $54$. What is the tens digit minus the units digit?

try.prompt: $(10a + b) - (10b + a) = k(a - b)$. What is $k$?

cards.title: Equations with digits
cards.body: Turn the words into an equation in $a$ and $b$, simplify, then list the digit pairs that fit. "A number is $4$ times its digit sum" gives $10a + b = 4(a + b)$, so $6a = 3b$ and $b = 2a$.

cards.title: Worked example: four times the digit sum
cards.problem: How many two-digit numbers are $4$ times the sum of their digits?

steps.text: $b \leq 9$, so $a$ is $1, 2, 3$ or $4$: the numbers $12, 24, 36, 48$. That is $4$ numbers.

try.prompt: How many such numbers are there?

cards.title: The common trap: digits have limits
cards.body: Each digit is at most $9$, and the first digit can't be $0$. Check every candidate against these limits before you count. And $10a + b$, not $a + b$, is the number itself.

prompts: Why is a number minus its reversal always a multiple of $9$?
